job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Dana Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up at half six in a shared house in Leicester with two students, and I take the bus to a payroll bureau on an industrial estate. I'm a payroll clerk, so I run weekly and monthly pay for about 40 small employers, like garages, a dental practice and a bakery. It's a lot of checking hours, tax codes and holiday pay, and I keep a paper checklist beside the screen because I don't trust myself otherwise.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how did you end up there?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied accounting at a university in the East Midlands and got a good result. My internship was in the accounts office of a tyre-fitting firm, which is how I learned payroll. My mum works at a pharmacy counter and covers my rent when I'm short, and I have a younger brother, Yusuf, who's 17 and still at school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's fine, a bit of help with some forms. We already have software that calculates tax, so a little more of it isn't a big shock. I'd tell friends that nothing really changes and we can all calm down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think routine payroll runs are exactly what gets nibbled at, even in a slow version. The bureau already took away one admin job last year. I'd be fine for now, but I'd keep an eye on the clients leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and try to be the careful one, the person who never makes mistakes. I'd save 100 a month and keep my checklist and my routines. I'd ask for a pay rise after my first year and see what the manager says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, but not comfortable. I have loans and rent, and my pay is quite normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bureau already lost one admin job. What happened there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Her name was Pat, and she did the filing and the envelopes. When the clients moved to online payslips, nobody needed her. She was 55, and they gave her a small payoff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that make you think about your own job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, though I try not to dwell. I tell myself I do real checking, not envelopes. But if the clients started doing their own pay with the software, I'd be the next one to lose my job. Like Pat.

say: I'd say it's a **bit of help** and nothing really changes.
I'd tell friends we can all **calm down**.
think: Routine payroll runs are exactly what gets **nibbled** at, even in a slow version.
The bureau already cut one **admin job** last year.
do: Carry on and be the **careful** one who never makes mistakes.
Save **100 a month** and keep my paper checklist.
Ask for a **pay rise** after the first year.
feel: A bit **uneasy**, with loans, rent and ordinary pay on my mind.
S0.quote: I tell myself I do real checking, not envelopes. But if the clients started doing their own pay with the software, I'd be the next one to lose my job.
fieldNote: Dana's worry is built on a **real example**: a colleague, Pat, who lost her filing job.
She reassures herself with the word checking, but knows the line is thin.
Resistant to change; her paper checklist is a symbol of that.

steps.text: Keep running payroll for the small employers using the paper checklist
Save 100 a month towards three months of rent
Ask the manager about a pay rise after the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say I'm not sure we're ready, and I'd ask what the firm's plan is. I'd tell my mum I'm worried about payroll, because that's the sort of thing software can calculate and check. Online I'd mostly read and not post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is on the list. Payroll is checking numbers against rules, and that's the thinking work the card talks about. I'd expect the bureau to keep fewer clerks and give the rest more clients each.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably wait for the firm to tell us what to learn, but I'd also sign up for an evening course in bookkeeping and tax advice, about 35 a week, so I can talk to clients and not just run reports. I'd ask my manager, Nasreen, whether I could take on the client calls. And I'd save 150 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not panicking, but I'd be awake at 2am doing sums about how long my savings would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for the firm. What if it doesn't tell you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd feel stuck, to be honest. I don't like new technology and I'm slow with it. But I'd force myself to ask Nasreen directly, and I'd start the course anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the course really about the technology, or about avoiding it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both, I suppose. I'd rather learn the human side, talking to clients about their tax, than become a tool person. But I know I might end up needing both.

say: I'd say I'm not sure we're **ready** and ask for the firm's plan.
I'd tell my mum payroll is the kind of thing **software** checks.
think: Payroll is checking numbers against **rules**, which is the thinking work on the card.
I expect fewer clerks with **more clients** each.
do: Sign up for an evening **tax and bookkeeping** course at about 35 a week.
Ask my manager, Nasreen, if I can take the **client calls**.
feel: **Anxious**, awake at 2am doing sums about how long savings would last.
S1.quote: I'd rather learn the human side, talking to clients about their tax, than become a tool person.
fieldNote: Dana picks the **human side** of the job over tools, which fits her resistance.
She admits she might need both, a sign of honest self-doubt.
Her coping style is to wait, then force herself to ask.

steps.text: Enrol in an evening tax and bookkeeping course
Ask manager Nasreen to let me take client calls
Save 150 a month for six months of cover

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nothing at first, I'd just feel sick. Then I'd ask the manager for a straight answer. Online, I'd probably share articles about what governments should do, because I don't know what else to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job disappears. Everything I do is thinking work, with rules and numbers, and the machine would do it cheaper. I'd be one of the first, and I'd have no idea what else I'm good for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost I could, about 200 a month, and tell my mum early that I might need to move back home. I'd start looking at jobs in hands-on work, like a pharmacy assistant or something in a hospital office, since robots take a few more years to reach them. And I'd ask for help with how to learn something, because I'd be lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I'd feel like the ground has been taken away, and I'd be ashamed to say that to my brother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel ashamed. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Yusuf looks up to me. I'm the one who went to university and got a proper job. I'd feel I'd let the family down, even though it's nobody's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody in particular. The firms do what they do to cut costs. The government should have planned ahead, but they never plan for anything. So mostly I'd feel unlucky.

say: I'd say nothing at first, then ask the manager for a **straight answer**.
I'd share articles about what **governments** should do.
think: My job **disappears**, since everything I do is rules and numbers.
I'd have no idea what else I'm **good for**.
do: Cut about **200 a month** and warn my mum I might move home.
Look for **hands-on** work such as a pharmacy assistant or hospital office.
Ask for help to **learn** something new.
feel: **Scared**, as if the ground was taken away, and ashamed in front of my brother.
S2.quote: I'm the one who went to university and got a proper job. I'd feel I'd let the family down, even though it's nobody's fault.
fieldNote: Dana's fear is tied to **family pride**, especially her brother Yusuf.
She blames nobody in particular, a pragmatic centre view.
Her plan is thin, which she knows.

steps.text: Cut about 200 a month from spending
Move back to my mum's home to save rent
Apply for pharmacy assistant and hospital office jobs
Ask my manager and a careers adviser how to learn something new

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not nothing, but it's not long either. At work I'd ask the firm what happens to juniors, and I'd say we should all get training now and not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be anxious but with a little breathing room. In five years I'd be 27, and I could build something. My problem is that I'd probably put it off, because I'm someone who waits for a push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the tax and bookkeeping course and aim for a role talking to clients, maybe at an accounting practice. I'd save 250 a month, since I'd have time to build a proper cushion. I'd also ask my mum if I can learn from how the pharmacy deals with customers, because that's the human side I want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than with two years. It feels like a deadline I can see, even if I'm not ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably put it off. How would you stop yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nasreen my deadline, so she can ask me about it. I'm much better when someone else is waiting. If it's just in my head, I'll find a reason to start next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make five years feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I knew there was money for retraining and that employers would still want people for the client side. A promise from someone official would help, even a small one.

say: I'd say five years is **not nothing**, but not long either.
I'd ask the firm what happens to **juniors** and ask for training now.
think: I'd be anxious but with some **breathing room**, since I'd be 27.
I would probably **put it off**, because I wait for a push.
do: Finish the tax and bookkeeping **course** and aim for a client-facing role.
Save **250 a month** to build a proper cushion.
Learn **customer** skills from how my mum's pharmacy works.
feel: **Anxious**, but less sick than in the two-year world.
S3.quote: I'm much better when someone else is waiting. If it's just in my head, I'll find a reason to start next month.
fieldNote: Dana knows her own **habit** of delay and plans a way around it.
She wants an official promise of retraining money.
The pharmacy idea is her take on the human side of work.

steps.text: Finish the tax and bookkeeping course within a year
Save 250 a month towards a six-month cushion
Apply to accounting practices for client-facing roles

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and by then there will be training and new jobs. At work I wouldn't say much, and online I'd stay quiet. I'd talk to my brother about what he should study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still anxious, but it's more a background hum. In ten years I'd be 32 and could be doing something quite different. My fear is that I'll assume I've got time, and then wake up with three years left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my qualifications and try to move into advisory work at a practice. I'd also learn at least one tool properly, after years of avoiding them, because by then everyone will use them. And I'd help Yusuf pick a course, perhaps nursing or something with people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. It's like knowing a storm is coming next decade, so I'd still do my shopping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn one tool properly. What would push you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A boss who set the time aside, honestly. Or a friend who showed me in person. I learn better with a person than with a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't follow money, follow what you'd still enjoy at 40. And whichever job it is, learn to talk to people, because that bit lasts.

say: I'd say ten years is **long enough** for training and new jobs to arrive.
I'd talk to my brother about what he should **study**.
think: I'm still anxious, but it's a **background hum**.
My fear is assuming I have time and waking up with **three years** left.
do: Finish my **qualifications** and move into advisory work.
Learn **one tool** properly because everyone will use them by then.
Help my brother **Yusuf** pick a course, maybe nursing.
feel: **Mostly okay**, like knowing a storm is coming next decade.
S4.quote: My fear is that I'll assume I've got time, and then wake up with three years left.
fieldNote: Dana's anxiety is about **her own habits**, not the date.
She wants a person to teach her, not a screen.
Her advice to Yusuf, learn to talk to people, mirrors her own plan.

steps.text: Finish the accounting qualification and move into advisory work
Learn one AI tool properly with a colleague showing me
Help Yusuf choose a college course with people in it

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my whole job is what the machine would do best. What would help is a clear warning from the firm, paid time to learn something new, and some kind of help with the rent while I do. I'd also need someone to show me where to start, because I wouldn't know.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'm scared of the technology itself. I'm not scared of the technology, I'm scared of being told to use it with no training, and then being blamed when the numbers are wrong.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the technology, I'm scared of being told to use it with no training, and then being blamed when the numbers are wrong.
portrait: Dana, 22, is a **payroll clerk** at a bureau in Leicester, running pay for about 40 small employers.
She shares a house, has loans, and her mum covers the **rent** if she's short.
Centre in her views and resistant to change, she keeps a **paper checklist** and never uses AI tools.
Her mood runs from uneasy to **alarmed** at two years, but her fear is mostly about being unprepared.
Her little brother Yusuf and her mum, who works at a pharmacy, are her anchors.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because payroll is what the machine does best and she'd not know where to start.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **warning**, paid time to learn something new and help with rent while she does.
